facts.claim: Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World, Cal Newport, 2016. DB title 'Konsantrasyon Gücü' (2020) could not be matched to a Turkish edition; the Turkish edition found is 'Pürdikkat' (Metropolis, 2019). All stories rest on Deep Work.

Newport defines deep work as professional activities performed in a state of distraction-free concentration that push cognitive capabilities to their limit, create new value, improve skill and are hard to replicate.

Shallow work: non-cognitively demanding, logistical-style tasks, often performed while distracted, such as answering email, attending status meetings, filling out forms; they tend not to create much new value and are easy to replicate.
Newport's formula: High-Quality Work Produced = (Time Spent) x (Intensity of Focus).
Sophie Leroy (2009 paper 'Why Is It So Hard to Do My Work?') introduced attention residue: after switching from task A to task B, part of your attention stays on A.
The residue is thickest when the work on task A was unbounded and low in intensity.

In Leroy's lab studies participants solved word puzzles, were interrupted to evaluate resumes, then took a quick lexical decision test to measure leftover residue. People with attention residue performed worse on the next task; more residue meant worse performance.
Newport says experts max out around four hours of deep work a day, beginners far less.
Ritualizing: decide where you will work and for how long; set rules for the session (no internet, or an output target); prepare support (food, drinks, a walk before starting).
Newport describes four scheduling philosophies: monastic, bimodal, rhythmic and journalistic; Carl Jung is cited as a bimodal example.
Carl Jung began building the Bollingen Tower retreat in 1922; Newport's point is that Jung retreated there to advance his work, not to escape it.
Bill Gates took 'Think Weeks' twice a year, isolating himself (often in a lakeside cottage) to read and think; in a 1995 Think Week he wrote the 'Internet Tidal Wave' memo.
Darwin kept a strict structure while perfecting On the Origin of Species: as his son Francis remembered, he rose promptly at seven to take a short walk, and worked in his study about 8 to 9:30.

rejected.claim: Typical knowledge workers get one to two hours of deep work a week/day (measured).
rejected.reason: No such figure found in the book.

rejected.claim: An interrupted knowledge worker needs on average 23 minutes to regain focus; ten interruptions cost 230 minutes.
rejected.reason: Not attributable to Deep Work (comes from other research).

rejected.claim: Karl Marx worked at the same desk in the British Museum; Woody Allen the same typewriter every day.
rejected.reason: Not found in Deep Work sources.

rejected.claim: Open offices and constant notifications are enemies of deep work (Newport quote).
